chapters.summary: Council staff welcomes attendees to the joint hearing of the Committee on Veterans and the Committee on Mental Health and Substance Use, and reminds attendees to put devices on silent.
chapters.title: Staff opens hearing with housekeeping announcements

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome to the New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Veterans, joined with the Committee on Mental Health and Substance Use.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please put all devices on silent.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Anyone wishing to testify or have any questions, please see one of the sergeants at arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Going forward, no one is to approach the desk.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

chapters.summary: Chair Morano introduces himself, reflects on the value of committee hearings, and cites past hearings on post-9/11 veterans, LGBTQ+ veterans, veterans of color, and female veterans that produced concrete legislation.
chapters.title: Chair Morano opening: value of committee hearings and past work

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Frank Morano.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I have the privilege of being the chair of the Committee on Veterans.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us today for our oversight hearing with the Committee on Mental Health and Substance Abuse.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And you will hear from their distinguished chairperson in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I'm very, very much looking forward to today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I really can't say enough about the value that I think these hearings have had since I've been lucky enough to chair this committee.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You know, New Yorkers, as many people know, are cynical.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And if possible, Staten Islanders that I represent can be the most cynical of a cynical group.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And oftentimes when it comes to the public and, quite frankly, even a lot of legislators, there's a lot of head scratching about what these hearings actually accomplish.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm not necessarily talking about this committee, but any of these hearings in general.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: There's the feeling that, in fact, I said this today multiple times, there's a feeling that there's a lot of grandstanding politicians

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: asking questions to a lot of stonewalling bureaucrats, and it's not necessarily clear what's being moved forward.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I really do think that the committee hearings that we've held have stood in stark contrast to that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Not only the testimony that we've gotten from the administration, not only the reports that the committee.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: has prepared, but the dynamic testimony from the public, including the public, by the way, who is occasionally critical of the work that this council's been doing on veterans affairs.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Whether it's been the hearing that we had on post-9-11 veterans, whether it's been the hearings that we've had on LGBTQ plus veterans, whether it's been the roundtable that we did on

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: veterans of color, whether it's been the hearing and associated roundtable that we've done on post-9-11 veterans or on female veterans,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: each of those hearings has produced concrete legislation that I am looking forward to introducing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In some cases, I have introduced.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I think it really does lay the groundwork for actually improving the lives of the large number of veterans that live in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I'm hopeful that this hearing that we're going to undertake today, which is on a very important issue, does that same thing.

chapters.summary: Morano reviews the October 2024 PTSD hearing, Local Laws 37-40 of 2024, and reveals that far too many city agencies are not in compliance with Local Law 37, which requires identifying veterans when they interact with city agencies.
chapters.title: Morano on recent history: Local Laws 37-40 and agency non-compliance

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit about some of the recent history that we're going to be exploring today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In October of 2024, these committees examined the city's efforts to support veterans and their families impacted by PTSD.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: At that time, New York City's Department of Veteran Services highlighted its family outreach efforts, their mental health programs, and resource navigation services, while local laws 37th.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: 38, 39, and 40 of 2024 had just taken effect.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The council is eagerly awaiting reporting required under Local Law 37, which is intended to help identify veterans when they interact with city agencies and connect them to available services.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One spoiler alert for the public, far too many city agencies are not in compliance with Local Law 37.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're going to find out.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Who the biggest offenders are, and we're going to find out what we're going to do about why they're not in compliance.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The city has issued reports under local law 39, but participation and data quality remain concerns.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Only 10 agencies reported data in fiscal year 2024, and only seven agencies reported quantitative data in fiscal year 2025.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So while veteran identification has improved, the city still lacks consistent data on whether veterans who request mental health services ultimately receive care,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: limiting the council's ability to assess service access and outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: These gaps are especially important as veterans continue to face many of the same challenges as other New Yorkers, including housing instability, affordability pressures, bureaucratic barriers, and the stigma

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: that's associated with seeking mental health support.

chapters.summary: Morano presents veteran population data: 637,542 veterans in New York State, about 122,700 in New York City. He describes the complex psychological impacts of military service including PTSD, substance use, and behavioral health issues.
chapters.title: Morano on veteran population statistics and mental health impacts

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Now, let me tell you a little bit about the situation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: involving veterans in New York in terms of the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: According to the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Department of Veterans Affairs, New York State ranks ninth in total veteran population.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In 2024, there were nearly 18 million veterans in the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And 637,542 residing in New York State, with about 122,700 living in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When we look at and explore the effects of military service on veterans'psychological health, there are so many different aspects to look at.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And it's one of the reasons why I think veterans'issues really affect the issues that every single city agency deals with.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The impacts of military service on psychological health, as you might guess, are quite complex.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And as a result, veterans tend to suffer from substance and alcohol use and misuse, sexual trauma, behavioral health issues, and mental health disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorders.

chapters.summary: Morano details barriers to care including difficulty navigating the behavioral health system, stigma, geographic barriers, and the need for cross-cultural competency training for female, LGBTQ+, and minority veterans.
chapters.title: Morano on barriers to mental health and substance use care

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Now, what are the key barriers to mental health and substance use care among veterans in New York State?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Veterans in the state continue to experience significant unmet mental health and substance use treatment needs despite high rates of health insurance coverage and access to VA benefits.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Think about that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Even when people have insurance and are covered, they're still having difficulty.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: for whatever reason, either accessing or taking advantage of the benefits that they're legally entitled to and that the taxpayers are paying for them to receive.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: This gap in treatment is due to a lot of challenges, including difficulty navigating the behavioral health system and understanding available benefits, negative stigma in some quarters towards treatment,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: geographic and logistical barriers, and increasing need for equity and cross-cultural competency training

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: to better identify the needs of female veterans, LGBTQ plus veterans, and veterans from racial and ethnic minority backgrounds.

chapters.summary: Morano raises concerns about the VetConnect NYC portal since 2018, citing difficulties with access, navigation, and follow-up, and references Comptroller Mark Levine's recent audit report.
chapters.title: Morano on VetConnect NYC portal concerns and Comptroller audit

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Now, with all that in mind, we have heard a great deal of late about VetConnect NYC.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Veterans, advocates, and nonprofit providers and city council members have regularly raised concerns about the VetConnect NYC portal site since its inception in 2018.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Users continue to face difficulties accessing and navigating the portal,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: reaching agency staff and caseworkers, and a lack of follow-up after seeking services, which has contributed to delayed access to services, including mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And that was spelled out recently in a report by the New York City Comptroller Mark Levine.

chapters.summary: Morano reads a statement from Councilmember Areola about Resolution 493, which would declare April 7 as White Star Family Day, recognizing families who lost a service member or veteran to suicide.
chapters.title: Morano reads Councilmember Areola's statement on Resolution 493: White Star Family Day

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In addition to our oversight topic today, we're going to be hearing about resolution.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Number 493, which is sponsored by Councilmember Areola, which would declare April 7th as White Star Family Day in the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Now, because we do not, Councilmember Areola just messaged me that she actually doesn't have a link to log on,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: but she did send me this statement to read on her behalf about Resolution 493.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: She says, Resolution 493 addresses an important gap in how we recognize families who have lost a service member or veteran to suicide.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: White Star families carry a loss that is often deeply painful, and unlike Gold Star families, they currently have no formal designation or official recognition specifically acknowledging their service.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: This resolution is about making sure these families aren't overlooked and that their loss is recognized with the dignity and respect it deserves.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Our veterans and service members dedicate themselves to protecting our country, and our commitment to them should not end when their service ends.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We must also recognize and support the families who are left behind, particularly those facing the unique grief, stigma, and challenges associated with suicide loss.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: By declaring April 7th as White Star Family Day in New York City, we are taking a meaningful step towards bringing greater awareness.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: to veteran suicide and ensuring that the families affected by it know that their loss has not been forgotten.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I urge my colleagues to join me in recognizing these families and supporting Resolution 493.

chapters.summary: Morano acknowledges Councilmembers Wong and Aldebol, and praises co-chair Caban for her intelligence and willingness to work across ideological lines on veterans and mental health issues.
chapters.title: Morano acknowledges colleagues and praises co-chair Caban

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Now, I want to acknowledge my colleagues on both committees who are here today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The man who I believe still has perfect committee attendance or pretty close to it, the distinguished council member from Queens, Phil Wong, is here, as well as council member Al DeBall from the Boogie Down Bronx is here as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Before I conclude, I would like to acknowledge Councilmember Caban, the chair of the Committee on Mental Health and Substance Abuse, for working with me on this oversight hearing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: She recognizes as much as I do how crucial it is to address the mental health issues veterans face and the barriers to treatment that many still experience.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to just reiterate how genuinely privileged and fortunate I am to be able to co-chair this hearing with Councilmember Caban.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you were to try to find the two council members that probably have the least similar voting records in our council, it would probably be Councilmember Caban and me.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: At yesterday's hearing and I think at the one that we were just at, the C's

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: on the far right facing the witness table was occupied by me, and the seat on the far left facing the witness table was occupied by her.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I don't know that that was an accident.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I will tell you, one of the reasons I was so eager to co-chair this hearing with Councilmember Caban is I think by the two of us

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: co-chairing this hearing together, not only do I think we usually ask the best questions in all the hearings, but I think it sends such a powerful message about mental health and substance abuse and veterans issues specifically, that

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: not only is this not a partisan issue, but you could take the people representing the folks in the city that are furthest to the right and furthest to the left

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: and show that their representatives care about this issue just as deeply, even if we end up having somewhat different solutions in terms of how to address it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I think addressing it to begin with is really the first hurdle that we as New Yorkers need to overcome.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You know, in the pro-wrestling world that politics and government often seems, a lot of times you're cautioned, oh, you don't want to be seen with this person.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You don't want to be seen working with this person.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Not only do I find Councilmember Caban to be one of the most intelligent and hardworking members of this body, but I think the mentality that I just described is...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: is exactly the problem in politics and government these days.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I want to find the people that I disagree with the most, and those are the folks that I want to work with the most on the issues that we both care about.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I was warned that Councilmember Caban was the nicest member of this council when I was elected, and those warnings have turned out to be true.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I'm excited that she is able to co-chair this hearing with me.

chapters.summary: Morano thanks committee staff including legislative counsel Hannah Cohn, senior counsel Sarah Sucher, legislative analyst Raina Lee, policy analysts Mahnoor Boot and Justin Campos, financial analyst Sandra Gray, and community associate Sebastian Neme.
chapters.title: Morano thanks committee and personal staff

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I also want to thank the committee staff.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Our outgoing legislative counsel, Hannah Cohn, our senior legislative counsel, Sarah Sucher, our legislative analyst, Raina Lee, making her debut.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm very, very excited to have Raina here.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And Raina, I think that you'll find that when we go through legislative analysts,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: quickly here.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Hopefully it's not because I'm difficult to work with, but I'm committed to, while we're working together, really leaving an impact on veterans issues in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm excited to work with you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Legislative policy analysts, Mahnoor Boot and Justin Campos, who, as always, have just been incredible.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Financial analyst, Sandra Gray, and community associate and someone who's absolutely indispensable in all the work this committee does, Sebastian Neme, for their hard work.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: in preparing for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I also want to thank my staff for their work as we continue to serve our constituents and the city as a whole,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: particularly my chief of staff, Frank Rapacciolo, but also my director of communications, Alexis Winters, who's here today and hails from the great borough of Queens, the borough with the highest percentage of veterans

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: in our city.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Alexis.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm looking forward to today's testimony and to strengthening support veterans facing accessing mental health and substance abuse services throughout New York City.

chapters.summary: Morano addresses Q&A format, encouraging colleagues to ask follow-up questions without worrying about the five-minute buzzer, and announces he will yield to other members before returning for additional questions.
chapters.title: Morano on Q&A format and procedural flexibility

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And just one quick note for the public and our colleagues, Council Members Wong and Aldeball.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You know, we just left a hearing, and I was there for two hours, and literally the only people that got to ask questions were the chairs of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It's no criticism of them, but you had a lot of very intelligent council members

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: that worked very hard on preparing questions for the panel that was appearing before us, and they didn't get to ask any questions because they couldn't stay for longer than two hours.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So after the testimony from DVS, I'm going to ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Presumably Chair Cabana will ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And then I am going to wait and allow everybody else who has questions to ask them, and then I'll come back.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Also, the five-minute buzzer drives me crazy.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Council members feel like they're playing beat the clock to ask a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you're asking questions and the DVS folks are nice enough to give a thoughtful, comprehensive answer and you have an appropriate follow-up question, ask it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Ask it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Don't worry about the buzzer going off.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Just ask it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It's fine.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You don't have to ask permission.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Just go ahead and ask it with my blessing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're going to have as close to an organic conversation as we can on this.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I would now like to turn it over to our committee counsel to administer the...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Oh, well, all right.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Well, it's not in my script.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I don't know what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Before we swear in our distinguished panelists today, please welcome the chair of our co-committee today, Councilmember Caban.

chapters.summary: Chair Caban welcomes veterans, families, and advocates, noting that Queens has the highest concentration of veterans. She highlights elevated rates of PTSD, depression, anxiety, and suicide among veterans and the ripple effects on military families and caregivers.
chapters.title: Chair Caban opening: veteran mental health crisis and family impact

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And just echo the sentiments that you talked about previously.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We're, you know, willing to work with anybody who wants to solve a problem.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So that's what we're here to do.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm excited to be talking about this topic today.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I want to very quickly recognize that we have been joined by Councilmember Areola on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We have also been joined by Councilmember Aldebal.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Oh, we already did her.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Well, I recognize you twice.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I'd like to recognize Councilmember Wong again, too.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So my name is Councilmember Tiffany Kaman.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm the chair of the New York City Council's Committee on Mental Health and Substance Abuse.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I want to welcome our veterans, their families, caregivers, service providers, and advocates who have joined us today.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Many of you took time away from work, caregiving, or your own recovery to be here.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Your presence matters, and your testimony will shape the committee's work going forward.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: New York City is home to more than 170,000 veterans and hundreds of thousands more family members and caregivers whose lives are shaped by military service.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: These are New Yorkers who served, often at great personal cost, and who came home to a city that owes them real, accessible, and effective care.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: My home borough of Queens.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Like the chair mentioned, has the highest concentration of veterans in our city.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And veterans experience post-traumatic stress, depression, anxiety, and moral injury at rates significantly higher than the general population.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Suicide remains a devastating crisis in the veteran community nationally, and every one of those deaths reflects a failure somewhere.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: In our systems of care.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Substance use, often a form of self-medication for untreated trauma, disproportionately affects veterans and can compound housing instability, family breakdown, and further mental health decline.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: This crisis doesn't stop with the veteran alone.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Military families carry their own trauma, living with the ripple effects of deployment, reintegration, and often an unseen, undertreated condition in someone that they love.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Caregivers frequently sacrifice their own economic security and mental health to provide care, often without adequate support or recognition.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And if we're serious about veteran mental health, we have to be serious about family and caregiver.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: mental health too.

chapters.summary: Caban discusses veterans experiencing homelessness and those involved in the criminal legal system, drawing on her experience as a public defender. She emphasizes that untreated mental health and substance use needs are often at the root of homelessness and incarceration.
chapters.title: Caban on homeless, incarcerated veterans and system failures

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I also want to acknowledge veterans experiencing homelessness and veterans involved in our criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I was a public defender for a long time and a lot of our clients that, you know, came in persistently and consistently on low-level offenses that were born out of housing insecurity, mental health issues, substance use issues,

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: a lot of them were veterans.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And it's, again, that is another indication of the failure in our systems of care.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: In both cases, untreated mental health and substance use needs are often at the root of how someone ended up unhoused or incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Veterans should never fall through the cracks between city, state, and federal systems.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But too often, that's exactly what happens.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: A veteran in crisis may end up in our shelter system or in police custody, rather than with someone trained in trauma-informed veteran-competent care.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: This points to a larger truth.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Mental health care cannot be delivered in isolation from the rest of a veteran's life.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's inseparable from whether they have stable housing, income, transportation, and providers who actually talk to one another.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Housing instability in particular is both the cause and consequence of untreated mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: A veteran facing eviction is far less likely to keep a therapy appointment or stay in therapy, no matter how good that treatment is on paper.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And the same is true of food insecurity, unemployment, and lack of transportation.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: These aren't peripheral issues.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: They often determine whether a veteran can access care at all.

chapters.summary: Caban calls for accountability and action, asking agencies to share what is working and what is not, and asking veterans and families to share where the system failed them. She thanks staff and turns the mic back to Morano.
chapters.title: Caban on hearing goals: accountability and action

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And we don't intend this hearing to be a ceremonial exercise in a pre-

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: to our city's veterans.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We intend to produce accountability and action.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We want to hear from city agencies about what's working and more importantly about what's not and why.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And we want to hear directly from veterans and families about where the system failed them or simply wasn't there when they needed it the most.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So I want to thank the administration for being here, Chair Murano and my colleagues for their engagement, the advocates, veteran service organizations, families joining us, including those from my own district in Queens.
