chapters.summary: Commissioner Mata introduces herself as a veteran and soldier, describes the inaugural Remembrance Ruck across the Brooklyn Bridge with over 1,200 participants, and emphasizes that connection and community must be part of mental health approach.
chapters.title: Commissioner Mata testimony: Remembrance Ruck and community connection

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I'm Commissioner Mata for the Department of Veterans Services.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Murano, Chair Caban, and members of the Committees on Veterans and Mental Health for this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: My name is Yesenia Mata, and I serve as a commissioner of the New York City Department of Veterans Services.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today about the mental health and well-being of New York City's veteran community and the work we are doing to strengthen pathways to support.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: As a veteran and as a soldier, I know that asking for help is not always easy.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Military service teaches us resilience to accomplish the mission and to take care of the person standing beside us.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: But sometimes the person who is struggling is not the person who will raise their hand first.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: That is why our approach to veterans'mental health must begin before a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: It must begin with connection, community, early.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: intervention and trusted pathways to care.

chapters.summary: Mata presents data showing NYC veterans died by suicide at approximately twice the rate of civilians between 2012-2022, with concerning disparities among younger veterans. She outlines DVS's prevention approach focused on reducing isolation and strengthening social connection.
chapters.title: Mata testimony: veteran suicide data and prevention approach

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: This past Sunday, just two days after the 25th anniversary of September 11, more than 1,200 members of the military and veteran-affiliated community here in New York City

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: joined us for the city's inaugural Remembrance Ruck across the Brooklyn Bridge.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: The Ruck was first and foremost an act of remembrance, but it was also intentionally centered on camaraderie and community.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Veterans do not always come to DBS through a formal intake.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Process or because they have already identified a specific need.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Sometimes the first step is showing up, meeting another veteran, talking with a peer, or simply realizing there is a community around them.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: An event is not a substitute for clinical care, but it reinforces why connection and belonging must be part of our broader approach to mental health and suicide prevention.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: The data on veteran suicide underscore the urgency of this work.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Research examining veteran mortality in New York City between 2012 and 2022 found that veterans died by suicide at approximately twice the rate of the city's civilian population, with particularly concerning disparities among younger veterans.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Suicide prevention cannot belong to one program, one agency, or one level of government.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: For DVS, prevention means reducing isolation, strengthening social connection, identifying needs earlier, helping veterans navigate resources, and ensuring there is a

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: pathway to professional care when it is needed.

chapters.summary: Mata describes the first city-administered Joseph Dwyer program cycle in 2025, supporting 31 organizations across five boroughs, with 90% of participants likely to recommend the program. She notes 23 organizations are pre-qualified for the next cycle.
chapters.title: Mata testimony: Joseph Dwyer program funding and outcomes

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: With funding from New York State, DVS launched its first city-administered Joseph DeWire cycle in 2025, supporting 31 veteran and community-based organizations offering free in-person programming across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Nearly three-quarters of survey participants strongly agreed that their program increased their sense of connection to other veterans.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Three-quarters said it supported their emotional well-being, and 90% said they would be very likely to recommend the DeWire program to another veteran.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: As we move into the next cycle, 23 organizations have already been pre-qualified, and our new partnership with Citizens Committee for New York City will help move resources to participating organizations while allowing DVS to remain focused on

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: program oversight, our veteran community, and outcomes.

chapters.summary: Mata describes Mission Vet Check, a partnership with New York Cares using trained volunteers for supportive check-in calls. Over 1,000 calls were made in the most recent outreach, connecting veterans to mental health, housing, food, and employment resources.
chapters.title: Mata testimony: Mission Vet Check outreach program

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We are also strengthening proactive outreach through Mission Vet Check.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Mission Vet Check operated...

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Operates in partnership with New York Cares uses trained volunteers to make supportive check-in calls to veterans across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Through our most recent outreach, more than 1,000 calls were made to New York City veterans, creating another opportunity to connect with DVS and resources related to mental health, housing, food, employment, benefits, and other needs.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Mission Vet Check is not a crisis line or replacement for professional mental care.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: It is another opportunity to connect.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Listen, identify a need, and help a veteran understand where support is available.

chapters.summary: Mata describes the Veterans Mental Health Coalition, which convenes practitioners, researchers, and advocates to discuss emerging research, identify barriers to care, and strengthen relationships across the veteran mental health ecosystem.
chapters.title: Mata testimony: Veterans Mental Health Coalition

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Coordination across the mental health community is equally important.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Through the Veterans Mental Health Coalition, DVS convenes mental health practitioners, researchers, and advocates, organizational leaders, and veterans serving partners to discuss the issues affecting veterans and military families.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: These conversations allow us to examine emerging...

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: research, identify barriers to accessing care, discuss programs and treatment models, and strengthen relationships across the veteran mental health ecosystem.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: No single organization has every answer.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Our role is to help build a network where veterans do not have to navigate these systems alone.

chapters.summary: Mata acknowledges the Comptroller's VetConnect audit findings, states DVS generally agrees with recommendations, and is taking steps to strengthen performance standards, vendor accountability, and reporting. She emphasizes VetConnect is one of multiple pathways to DVS.
chapters.title: Mata testimony: VetConnect NYC response to Comptroller audit

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: That is also why our navigation systems matter.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: The Comptroller's review of VetConnect identified areas where the system must improve, and we take those findings seriously.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: DVS generally agrees with the audit's recommendation and is taking steps to strengthen performance standards, vendor accountability, reporting, and opportunities for recurring feedback from veterans and stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: At the same time, VetConnect is one pathway to DVS.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: It is not the only pathway.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Veterans reach us online by phone, email, at events through our borough-based veteran resource centers, through Mission VetCheck, and through direct engagement with community.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: partners.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Technology should make accessing support easier, not become a barrier to it.

chapters.summary: Mata discusses coordination across city government, including partnership with DOHMH, and emphasizes that mental health cannot be delivered in isolation from housing, employment, food security, and family stability.
chapters.title: Mata testimony: cross-agency coordination and DOHMH partnership

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Our work also requires coordination across cities.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Government mental health does not exist in isolation from housing, employment, food security, benefits, physical health, or family stability.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We continue to work with partners across the administration, including the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, to strengthen connections between veterans and available services.

chapters.summary: Mata expresses administration support for Resolution 0493-2026 declaring April 7 as White Star Family Day, honoring families who lost a service member or veteran to suicide and continuing work to reduce stigma.
chapters.title: Mata testimony: support for White Star Family Day resolution

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Finally, as we discuss veteran suicide, we must also recognize the families who carry that loss.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: The administration supports Resolution 0493-2026, which would declare April 7th as White Star Family Day in the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Recognizing White Star families gives us an opportunity to honor families who have lost a service member or a veteran to suicide while continuing the important work of reducing

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: stigma around suicide, grief, mental health, and seeking help within the military and veteran community.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'm happy to answer any questions.

chapters.summary: Morano asks about the drop from 31 to 23 pre-qualified Dwyer organizations, whether boroughs including Staten Island are at risk of losing programs, and when funding will reach organizations. Mata and Chief of Staff Nicole Orlando explain the program is now being fully implemented and funded.
chapters.title: Morano Q&A: Dwyer program funding reduction from 31 to 23 organizations

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner, and thank you, as always, for your continuous outreach and communication, not only to me, but all the members of the Veterans Committee on Veterans Issues.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And congratulations on the Remembrance Ruck.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The only aspect that you didn't mention is that you had over 1,000 people participating and rucking across the Brooklyn Bridge in the rain the entire time.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I must say I was pretty impressed at your rucking ability, and I was glad to be there as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You testified that the city funded 31 organizations through the first Dwyer program.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: cycle, but only 23 organizations have been pre-qualified for the next cycle.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does that mean we're going to have fewer organizations providing services to veterans?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Are any boroughs, including our home borough of Staten Island, at risk of losing programs?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And when will the next round of funding actually reach those organizations?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I will pass this question shortly to my chief of staff, Nicole.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I would like to elaborate a bit on the history of this program.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: It first came out in FY25.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: However, it wasn't fully implemented, per se.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Organizations weren't fully funded because the program wasn't fully rolled out.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: However, under...

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: My tenure, this FY27th, this program is going to be fully rolled out, is fully going to be implemented, and the organizations will be receiving the full amount

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: if they were able to do great work without the full implementation or the funding before, they're going to be getting the most support this time around as it's going to be fully implemented and fully funded.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And I'll pass this question over to Nicole.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you for the question and thank you, committee.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: For the Dwyer programming in terms of those who have received the $20,000 funding in the previous Dwyer cycle to now, what we are working very closely is with our partners at MOX, as well as our friends over with Passport to ensure that all recipients of Dwyer

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: are able to take the appropriate steps to be pre-qualified and to receive this additional funding, as Commissioner stated, when it is fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So can you commit to providing the committee with a borough-by-borough comparison of the organizations funded in the first cycle and those funded in the next, including funding amounts and any gaps in service?

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So in terms of funding for the first cycle of Dwyer, each organization, no matter what borough it was in, received $20,000 in funding.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: That was the piloted Dwyer programming.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And we do have a breakdown borough by borough that we'd be happy to follow up with that is included in our Dwyer report.

chapters.summary: Morano asks how many veterans actually answered Mission VetCheck calls, how many identified mental health needs, and how many were connected to care. Orlando reports 27,544 calls since November 2025, with over 1,739 lasting more than 60 seconds.
chapters.title: Morano Q&A: Mission VetCheck call metrics and outcomes

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: On VetCheck, Commissioner, you testified that Mission VetCheck made more than 1,000 calls during its most recent outreach effort, and that's certainly encouraging.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many veterans actually answered those calls?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many identified a need for mental health services, and how many were successfully connected to care?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I guess what I'm trying to get at is, are we measuring the number of calls made, or are we measuring the number of veterans actually being helped?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And I'll pass that question on to my chief of staff, Nicole.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: But I do want to emphasize that under my tenure, we are revamping the mission vet check to ensure that we can even outreach to more veterans and fully provide that further service.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Since November of 2025, 27,544 mission vet check calls have occurred.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And within those calls, there was over 1,739 that lasted more than 60 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: By the way, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Orlando, I think this is the first time you've testified before this committee being introduced as chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I'm assuming that means congratulations are in order.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And the people of the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Are certainly well served with that.

chapters.summary: Morano asks which of the Comptroller's six VetConnect recommendations have been fully implemented, which remain outstanding, and when all six will be completed. Mata describes monitoring user experience, tracking service tickets, and incorporating public feedback.
chapters.title: Morano Q&A: VetConnect Comptroller recommendations status

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: On VetConnect, I'm sure my colleagues have a lot of questions about VetConnect, but just based on your

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: testimony, I definitely appreciate your acknowledgement of the controller's findings and your statement that technology should make accessing support easier and not become a barrier.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You said DVS is taking steps to strengthen performance standards, vendor accountability, and reporting.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Which of the controller's six recommendations have been fully implemented as of today, which remain outstanding, and when will all six be completed?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: As I cannot speak on the historical, per se, procurement decisions or

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: the context of that aspect, what I can say is that during my tenure here at DVS, I

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: have been regularly monitoring the VetConnect NYC user experience, tracking and following up on service tickets and incorporating public feedback.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And those are three of the recommendations as well that the comptroller recommended.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And with that, as we are doing that, I would like to also emphasize that under my tenure, we have developed the data department because data is very important for our agency.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I have a number of follow-up questions based on your testimony and a number of other

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: questions that the committee staff and I have worked on, but I will give Chair Caban and my colleagues an opportunity to ask some questions as well.

chapters.summary: Caban asks about major barriers to mental health care despite high insurance coverage. Mata and Orlando explain that one-third of staff are veterans, over two-thirds are military-affiliated, and all receive military cultural competency training. Family member eligibility for VA services is a key barrier.
chapters.title: Caban Q&A: barriers to mental health care and cultural competency

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'll also be brief so we can pass it over to colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So one thing that we've both addressed or brought up during our opening statements, sort of that there still exists some barriers to seeking and receiving care.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So I think I'm going to start with a line of questioning there.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You know, veterans in the state continue to experience significant unmet mental health and substance use treatment needs.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that is despite the high rates of health insurance coverage and access to VA benefits.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So like the coverage is there, the options are there, but there's a gap in treatment.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that's due to challenges, right?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's difficulty navigating the behavioral health system, understanding available benefits, negative stigma towards treatment, geographic and logistical barriers, increased need for

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: equity and cross-cultural competency training to better address the needs of women, of queer folks, veterans of different racial and ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So what are some of the major barriers?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: that kind of rise to the top when you're trying to assess health care coverage for mental and behavioral health services?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I'm going to be passing this question on to my chief of staff, but before that,

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: At DVS, we have different ways on how veterans can connect with us, whether it is through our social media platform, whether it is through our website, whether it is through our walkings or even VetConnect.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We understand that veterans like to be communicated, reached out.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Everyone has a specific way how they would like to be reached out.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So at DVS, what we are noticing is that, and we are aware, is that

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: if we are culturally competent, if a veteran doesn't, culturally military competent, if a veteran doesn't feel comfortable in the initiation to say, I am going through this or I'm suffering through this,

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: they may not want to disclose that.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: But because at DVS, our team is military culturally competent, eventually, because we create that safe space for the veteran, they end up disclosing

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: certain aspects of what they may be going through, whether it is mentally or physically.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And I'll pass on this question now.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Can I interject with just a follow-up for that before you continue?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So in terms of military culturally competent, how many of those volunteers are peers?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Like what's the ratio between just sort of a volunteer that's been trained in competency versus a peer volunteer?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: When you say volunteer, you mean in our agency that the staff?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Or the folks that are picking up the phones and assisting veterans when they call in.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I'm going to pass this question on to my chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Sorry, I added a question in there on top of the initial question.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So one-third of our staff are veterans.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: More than two-thirds are military affiliated, whether that be have a family member, be a spouse, be a Gold Star family member.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And all of our staff are military culturally competent and trained in that way, as well as up to date in their units on that training.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So what I mean by that is our claims team often goes to training that reinforces that, our housing team as well, and then also our social services department also.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And then in following up to the additional question about barriers to entry, what we would say is that since we don't only just serve the veteran population, we also serve veterans and their families as well.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So oftentimes a big barrier is eligibility criteria for family members because they cannot access VA services.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And I'll also pass over to Donnie.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm Donnie Smalls, Associate Commissioner for Housing and Supportive Services.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: We also have a model called Aftercare, where now we are, for housing, we use the Aftercare model.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: We are now branching over to mental health to shadow that Aftercare model.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: For mental health so that we can follow up with veterans that are, you know, going through mental health crisis, that we can follow up with them 24 hours,

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: two days, four days, a week after to make sure that, you know, they're seeking service and they got the services that they needed.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And just to add on what Associate Commissioner mentioned, the model now that we are implementing is mirroring per se the housing, the aftercare housing component.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Not just are we doing it within the mental health component, but across all services within the agency.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Caban asks about causes of veterans dropping out of therapy programs. Associate Commissioner Donee' Smalls describes the new Aftercare model with follow-up at 24 hours, two weeks, three months, and six months, and shares her peer-to-peer approach as a combat veteran.
chapters.title: Caban Q&A: therapy retention and Aftercare follow-up model

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So you mentioned some of the major barriers being family members and their eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We've also seen, and it's outlined in the committee report, interruption in programs and therapy.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So can you speak to some of the causes of veterans not being able to continue their therapy programs or dropping out of therapy programs?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: I think what we see also specific to mental health, but in the community in general, is just that continued engagement and different periods of the year where they may be more busy with life, with family, and we see that as an issue of not engaging in specific resources.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: I think from our perspective, and as Danae mentioned as well, is that is why we are increasing that follow-up so that if someone does fall off or maybe has, you know, is more quiet in times of the year, we can be sure to engage them again.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And what does that look like, that process of engagement?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Is there a sort of formula for, hey, this person missed one or two days, or there's a certain period of time they're gone, and then what does that engagement or follow-up look like?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: What amount of time?

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm going to pass over to Donnie to outline that.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Yes, so the detail, the model that we will follow is 24 hours after we connect veterans to services, we want to make sure that we follow up with them to see if they were engaged

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: or do they need further care.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Once that 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: comes, we have that communication.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: The veteran let us know, yes, we seek services.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: We're okay with the service provider that we're going.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Then we follow up with them two weeks later to make sure that they're still engaged in our services.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: From there, we will go three months, six months, or we build a communication and a relationship.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: with our veterans to where if they are falling off or if they need more help, they know that they can call us.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: We give a safe space, especially, well, I can't speak personally because I engage with the veteran community.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: I'm also a combat veteran.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Retired U.S.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Army.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: So I use my peer-to-peer skills that I have to engage with the veteran community, and I give them a safe space to talk

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: and feel comfortable that if they are going through crises or anything, that they could come back to not only me but my staff.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: And my staff, I trained them in the same way where, you know, they can have that safe space with their clients.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Where if anything is happening within the intervals of the aftercare program, that they could come back to us and we can get them back on track with the services that they need.

chapters.summary: Caban asks about connection rates during check-ins. Smalls reports a 50-50 connection rate initially, declining over time due to phone number changes. Orlando describes retention efforts through Dwyer participant surveys, social media growth from 3,000 to 6,000 followers, and a weekly newsletter.
chapters.title: Caban Q&A: connection rates, retention efforts, and outreach

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: When you're doing those check-ins, what's the connection rate like?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I also just want to acknowledge that obviously you're checking in on somebody who presumably was connected to an outside, and they have their own protocols for when somebody doesn't show up.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And then, again, I have a former colleague here that's going to testify, but putting my public defender hat on, some of the most simplest things.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's like, oh, why can't your client come back to court and complete the program?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Because they don't have a MetroCard.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Because they didn't feel like they could show up in clean clothes today.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Or just other things that are destabilizing their life that are, you know, are...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: That they can't keep up with.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: So the connection rate is, I'd say about 50-50.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Once we connect them to the outside.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: That's actually really good.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: As somebody who knocks doors or makes phone calls, that's a pretty high connection rate.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: In the interviews, the further out it is, the connection rate gets a little bit harder.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Because, of course, simple things like people changing phone numbers and not updating us with the information causes the reason why we can't connect at the later interviews.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: But within the first same year we have a strong connection with them.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And what are your retention effort?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Besides the check-in, is there anything else that you guys do to sort of encourage, promote retention in programs and services?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: What are the things that you're doing to reduce stigma?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And then to kind of round out this line of questions, are there identifiable services that...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: That we should be providing that?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Like, what are the gaps that you're seeing in terms of veteran retention and programming?

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: I think we have, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And I think we have learned a lot from the Dwyer programming.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So for the Dwyer programming that had run, we did a participant survey after each of the programs.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And a lot of the overwhelming feedback was that 90% were recommended to another veteran.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: 79% felt that they were encouraged.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: to seek other mental health support, as Dwyer is suicide prevention funding, but done in a way to facilitate peer-to-peer support and reduce social isolation.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: But they are reporting that since they were with that community, with each other, then they felt more empowered to get services.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Something that we've seen in the veteran community is that a lot is spread by word of mouth.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: That is something that still remains to be the greatest way to share information within the community.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So for us as an agency, what we've been focusing on is sharing that information in a multitude of ways.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So that includes creating our Veterans Resource Guide.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: To be in a Spanish version as well.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: That includes growing our social media from 3,000 followers to over 6,000 followers to ensure we're sharing information, as well as our weekly newsletter.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So that is something that we've seen the subscriber rate increase since prior to the commissioner's tenure here, it has now increased.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So for us, it's making sure that the information we're sharing is not in just one mechanism or one way.

chapters.summary: Caban asks about outreach campaigns and available languages. Mata describes the Dwyer program's varied activities across boroughs, marketing in multiple languages, and targeted roundtables with female veterans and LGBTQ+ veterans to determine best communication approaches.
chapters.title: Caban Q&A: outreach campaigns, languages, and targeted marketing

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So you mentioned the Instagram account and the weekly newsletter.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Can you talk about any other types of outreach or public awareness campaigns and also what languages they're available in?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Just the breadth of what's being done in terms of proactive outreach.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Well, thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: As I mentioned, I'm very happy to know that the WIRE program is going to be fully implemented this year and that the nonprofits will actually get the funding that they need and deserve in order to continue that work because

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: where when there are barriers oftentimes is because it's how can we better certain individuals be reached, but also communicated at.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And like, if you are not familiar with the Dwyer program, just to elaborate a little bit on that, the Dwyer program, it goes from dancing, it goes from yoga, it goes from like doing exercise.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: It's different ways that veterans are being reached in different boroughs, because even, for example, like myself, I am from Staten Island, and I...

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Communicate better in Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Like I know what, like we know our lingo, we know like if they say, oh go to Snug Harbor, I know where Snug Harbor is, right?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So it's an example that the beauty of this, the DeWire program is that it's going to be in all five boroughs and the groups are gonna be fully supported by getting the funding that they need.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And in addition to that, I believe a lot and the agency believes a lot on marketing and ensuring that not only do we have it on a specific language, but that we have it in different languages that we also reach out.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I know as a female veteran myself and a soldier myself, I also know that I want to be reached out differently when it comes to female veteran issues.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I also know when it comes to LGBTQ issues, I'd rather hear from the LGBTQ community themselves to let us know how they would like to be communicated at.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So marketing is important.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: However, we will not move forward with marketing without having those roundtables with those that are directly impacted to let us know how they want us to market.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Caban asks about top barriers and inter-agency coordination. Mata describes building bridges with 18-20 city agencies, up from three, and working on military cultural competency training. Orlando details partnerships with the Mayor's Office of People with Disabilities, Wounded Warrior Project, and DOHMH on borough hubs.
chapters.title: Caban Q&A: inter-agency coordination and DOHMH partnership

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And to wrap this line of questioning up, and then I'll hand it over to colleagues, it just...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Barriers, right?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Obviously, it includes housing instability.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It includes affordability.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It includes the difficulty navigating.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Is there anything that you think, again, just rises to the top that really, really needs to be focused on?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And then to your point, the intersection of a lot of different issues and communities, like what...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: How are you coordinating with other agencies or coordinating with housing, with benefits, with workforce, with social service agencies?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I'm going to pass this question to Nicole, but I'll elaborate on the agency component.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Since my tenure here, I've been working very closely on building bridges with various other city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I would like to emphasize that

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: as we do have allies, but unless you are a veteran yourself, unless you are a service member yourself, or are part of the military family per se, a military spouse, but even a Gold Star family or spouse, right?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Individuals or city agencies do need to be militarily, culturally trained or need to be provided guidance on how to best approach certain military issues.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So I have been working very diligently with city agencies on ensuring that, explain to them why veterans are important, why military families are important, Gold Star families are important.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So that's one.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: The second component is like Local Law 37, when it was introduced back in 2024, it hasn't been fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Only a few agencies have abided by that.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: But the other thing, too, that's why I mentioned military.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Cultural competency is that as a city agency, we also need to do that job to reach out and to train city agencies and to guide them.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So I've

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I would like to say that what went from three city agencies, we have now been in communication and in close partnership with 18 to 20.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And the goal is that on December when we report on that, you will see that huge jump.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And what does it look like specifically for DOHMH?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We have a very good relationship with DOHMH, but I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I'll have...

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Nicole, elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: I think before the DOHMH piece to also just with what Commissioner mentioned in terms of our agency collaboration as well as on the nonprofit and community-based organization side, a really good case study of this is the work that we do alongside the Mayor's Office of People with Disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: I think oftentimes that is a barrier to someone's accessibility to the things that are going on in the city or events or things of that nature, and we've formed a really strong partnership with the Mayor's Office of People with Disabilities as well as with the Wounded Warrior Project, specifically on our RUC,

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: to ensure that the route was completely accessible, to ensure that all the marketing materials was also accessible for those who have vision impairments.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So this is a great way that shows that we are bringing together all the partners, understanding that it doesn't belong to just one group.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And our collaboration with DOHMH has been very strong in terms of making sure the hubs that are in different boroughs are being utilized specifically by family members,

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: as well as the same thing on the front of marketing materials when they're speaking about mental health, ensuring that veterans'mental health is brought to the forefront.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Go ahead, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Morano acknowledges the 79th birthday of the U.S. Air Force and National POW/MIA Recognition Day, honoring generations of airmen and those who endured captivity, and encourages following DVS on social media for veteran commemorations.
chapters.title: Morano: Air Force 79th birthday and POW/MIA Recognition Day

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Before I go to my colleagues, I meant to acknowledge this earlier, but this is, I want to say, happy 79th birthday to the United States Air Force.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We thank the generations of airmen who served our country with courage and distinction.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And today also happens to be National POW MIA Recognition Day, when we honor those who endured captivity and remember the American service members who remain missing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We also recognize their families, many of whom have spent decades waiting for answers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I'll remind folks that if you want to know about any important veterans'commemorations or anniversaries within the city or state of New York, you should absolutely follow the Department of Veterans Services on social media.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: With that, I will ask my colleague, Councilmember Wong, to...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Ask away.

chapters.summary: Wong asks about DVS policy when contact is lost with a veteran. He shares that a constituent veteran committed suicide last year. Orlando describes maintaining multiple communication channels and consistent follow-up, including connecting with community-based organizations and federal VA partners.
chapters.title: Wong Q&A: losing contact with veterans and suicide prevention

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My first question to Commissioner Model is, what if you lose contact with a veteran?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Nobody picks up and then, no, doesn't mean it's anything bad.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They might be traveling or visiting families from another state.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So what's your policy when you lost contact with a veteran?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I'm going to pass that question to my chief of staff, but as I mentioned, at DVS, we have different ways for individuals to reach out to us.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Again, we're going to be doing a lot of work.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: whether social media, the website, intake process, walk-ins.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: But now during my tenure, we are creating that aftermath component that Dine had mentioned, and I'll pass on this question to Nicole.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: What we do here at DVS is ensure that we have more than one line of communication with the veteran.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So if we have their phone number, if we have their email address, text message, as well as any way that we can get in touch with them, consistent follow-up as well has proved to be super helpful.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: I think in that question as well, there has been times where our team has connected the community-based organization that they have been connected to or work closely with our federal partners on the VA level.

chapters.summary: Wong asks about longest wait times for mental health services at NYC veteran hospitals. Smalls describes vet centers in each borough as alternatives to VA hospitals, and referrals to nonprofits, Northwell Health, and Health and Hospitals. Wong expresses concern about waits of several weeks to months.
chapters.title: Wong Q&A: VA mental health wait times and alternatives

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking is that last year my constituents veteran unfortunately committed suicide and then

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I really, really feel that we can do better and we have to keep track of the veterans that live alone and has problems dealing with personal issues.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My next question is...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I understand in veteran hospitals there are wait time on certain health services.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question is which mental health services have the longest wait time at New York City veteran hospitals?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And what's the reason for these long waits?

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the time frame for the wait, but I

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: I do know that if we are not able to connect a veteran directly to the VA hospital, there are veteran centers in each borough where a veteran, we can connect a veteran to.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Those are entities, they partner with the VA, but they're outside.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: So you don't have to have VA health care to attend the VA health care.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Vet center in order to get help.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: And they have clinical clinicians there that can help a veteran in crisis.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: But we also help, I mean, we also refer to nonprofits.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: We also, outside providers, Northwell Health, health and hospitals, we refer veterans to as well.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It is my understanding that sometimes they can have to wait several weeks or even one or two months in order to get the service they need, and that's very frustrating when I hear about them.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And I hope that there's a system in place that they could go outside.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And get the services rather than wait two or three months, which to me is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: If I can also just jump in, I think an important piece too as us, as being the Department of Veteran Services, is that we do not provide that clinical support, so we do not provide that internal mental health counseling or relations, so we work a lot with our community partners to ensure there is that consistency.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And then in cases where there is an immediate need, we also leverage the 988 crisis line for that immediate need.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Immediate support.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And I've heard horror stories, your next appointment's in three months, and then when they need urgent care, they need it in a week, not three months.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: With that, I have a follow-up question.

chapters.summary: Wong asks about city-funded mental health programs for veterans and families. Orlando describes the Valone Initiative through VFW, which helps veterans file benefits claims related to mental health struggles. Wong requests data on how many people were helped.
chapters.title: Wong Q&A: city-funded mental health programs and Valone Initiative

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Are there any programs that the city council or the administration funds

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: that work on mental health services for veterans or their families.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: What we would say is that with the City Council discretionary funding, I think through the Valone initiative is one where veterans are able to then file for their benefits that in relation to any mental health struggles that they will be

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: experiencing, as well as since it is ran through the VFW, it also brings that camaraderie with a veteran service organization.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So although it may be indirectly, it does facilitate that support for a veteran community that is much needed.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Do you have data on how many people were helped by these programs?

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: For the level on initiative.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So we have that in our local 215 reporting.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So I'd be happy to follow up with it.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Jim.

chapters.title: Morano: requests Valone Initiative data by council district

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: By the way, when you get that information on the...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Ballone initiative and who's been helped by it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'd be interested in knowing since this is something that a lot of my colleagues and I spend a lot of time advertising as a service available to veterans in our district.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'd

utterances.text: I'd be curious if there's a breakdown by council district as well to see which council members are doing an effective job in terms of outreach and, you know, which council members maybe need a little help in making the service available to their constituents.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about age range breakdowns and reasons for disparities among younger veterans. Orlando reports the 18-34 age group has the highest suicide rate at 47.9 per 100,000. Mata discusses roundtables for younger veterans and collaboration with DYCD on transitioning service members and transferable skills.
chapters.title: Aldebol Q&A: younger veteran suicide disparities and outreach

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: With that, Council Member Aldebar.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you for testifying today.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs, for having this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony today that there's a particularly concerning disparities among younger veterans.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you have data on

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: couple of things.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What the breakdown is of the age ranges, the demographics, and

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: possible reasons why those disparities exist.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And are you working on tailoring both outreach and services for that particular group of veterans?

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So what we've seen on the national level, and we can definitely share this with you, I'll read some of the top lines as we understand it, is that in veteran suicide rate is twice the rate among non-veteran U.S.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Adults, as well as the age group of 18 to 34, which is typically our post-9-11 veterans, experience the highest suicide rate at 47.9 deaths per 100,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: These are the numbers that we are also actively tracking in collaboration with Intro 291 that was passed with DOHMH, as well as with our federal partners at the VA.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And I'm going to pass over to Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And to your point about younger veterans, that is something that as an agency, as I mentioned before, we continue hosting roundtables to ensure

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: that, again, that if there's messaging going to be targeted to younger veterans, what is the best approach?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I also want to indicate that I've been working very closely as well with the DYCD commissioner when it comes to have just conversations on what is the best approach when dealing, for an example, is a SYEP program, right?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I did, when I did meet with the DYCD commissioner, I did mention that oftentimes when younger veterans are transitioning out of the military, they're either 23 or about 23 years old, young veterans.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: They serve four years.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: But what happens when that young veteran transition?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: back to civilian world, what oftentimes happen is that military skills, your MOS per se, your job, right, that you have in the military,

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: when you transition back into the civilian world, oftentimes, like, civilians don't understand what your MOS was or the transferable skills that you have.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So we are trying to have those further discussions on what is the best way when those younger veterans as well transition back in the civilian world, how can their transferable skills of their MOS job per se

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: say, the civilians can understand, like, hey, this veteran, this young veteran has a specific skill, because oftentimes their skills are not transferable.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: When civilian employers look at their job, their background, they say, oh, well, they don't have a college degree, they haven't been in the civilian world, they don't have no training, not knowing that they do have the skills to lead, that they have the skills to manage.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So I think I just want to elaborate on that, because that's going to be another discussion in the future that we're going to be having.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: How do we best support those young veterans that also are returning back to ensure that they obtain employment?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Because oftentimes employment is one of the reasons why they go into substance abuse or even worse, commit suicide.

chapters.summary: A council member asks about connecting veterans to civil service employment. Orlando describes the 55A Pathways program, a state partnership for veterans with disability ratings, and a 2024 DCAS proposal allowing deployed service members to receive residency points on civil service exams.
chapters.title: Q&A: connecting veterans to civil service employment and 55A Pathways

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And what is your connection with connecting veterans to civil service employment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I know that, you know, they take civil service exams, they get extra points, but how do we get veterans more effectively into a civil service pipeline?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that they can actually access jobs and use those skills that in many ways can be transferable to the many hundreds of job titles in the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So that is something that we are very cognizant of at our agency, specifically with the utilization of the 55A Pathways program.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So that is something that we educate our veterans that we are seeing about to indicate on their resume and cover letter that they are 55A eligible.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: We have also worked with the state to ensure that a veteran who has a disability rating does not need to provide additional documentation to open up the case with AccessVR, where they are able to just be qualified for 55A.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: In addition to that, in 2024, we had a proposal accepted by DCAS that now for anyone who is serving active duty, they take their civil service exam.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: We were seeing this a lot with firefighters, cops who were taking the test.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And then since they were deployed during the time they needed to prove residency, they weren't also receiving the additional points for residency.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: The proposal that was accepted was that if they were from New York, but they couldn't prove that residency within the two years because they were deployed, they will continue to receive the residency points.

chapters.summary: Caban relays three questions from Councilmember Areola about DHS no longer pursuing VA Grant and Per Diem funding for transitional housing: how much funding is foregone, why DHS stopped, and how the administration will replace it. Orlando says DVS will follow up with DHS.
chapters.title: Caban relays Areola questions: DHS dropping VA Grant and Per Diem funding

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Before I get to Councilmember Wilson, Commissioner, I have a question from my colleague, Councilmember Areola, who's watching on Zoom but can't ask because we don't have a quorum here.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Councilmember Areola received a letter from the federal government indicating that the Department of Homeless Services is no longer pursuing funding through the VA's grant and per diem program, commonly known as GPD.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: For context, this program provides funding for transitional housing and supportive services for veterans experiencing homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So on her behalf, I have three questions.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: First, how much federal funding is the city foregoing?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Second, why has DHS decided not to pursue this grant?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And third, how does the administration intend to replace that funding and ensure that the veterans served by the program at Borden Avenue do not lose housing or supportive services?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And she adds, if DVS doesn't have those answers today, can you commit to coordinating with DHS and providing a written response to the committee and Councilmember Areola?

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: We, as the Department of Veteran Services, are separate of the federal VA and of DHS for these shelters, but what we can say is that we're remaining in close communication with all of our partners to ensure that our homeless veterans are taken care of, and we will follow up.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Councilmember Wilson.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks what happens when a veteran seeks housing assistance. Smalls describes the intake process: veteran housing coordinator assessment, housing plan development, subsidy assistance, and hand-in-hand support through permanent housing placement.
chapters.title: Wilson Q&A: housing assistance process for veterans

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Related to that topic, there's a pretty clear link between mental health and housing.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And I'm just curious, when a veteran comes to your department seeking assistance with housing, what happens next?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Is there a case manager or are they referred elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: For assistance?

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: So when a veteran comes to DBS for housing support, they do the initial intake.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: They speak with a veteran housing coordinator to see what their housing needs are.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: We come up with a housing plan for the veteran.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: We assess their needs, if they're able to pay, are they linked to the VA, do they have any housing subsidies that we can assist with, you know, finding them housing.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: If they don't have a housing subsidy, we walk them through the process hand in hand from the beginning to the end up until it's time for them to move into permanent housing.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks how many veterans are being worked with for housing and typical placement timelines. Smalls reports 209 veterans housed in FY26, the highest since the agency's inception, with typical timelines of three to six months depending on documentation like DD-214 availability.
chapters.title: Wilson Q&A: veterans housed and placement timelines

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How many veterans are you working with for housing assistance?

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Right now, I will have to get back to you with that number.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: What I can tell you is how many veterans that we house for FY26, we house over 209 veterans, which was the agency's most, the highest number that they house since conception.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And what's the typical time frame from someone who comes to your intake and then gets placed in housing?

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: That number, the amount of time can vary depending on documentation.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: If a veteran has documentation, sometimes a veteran might come, they don't have the DD-214, so that might take a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: So it could take anywhere between three to six months to house a veteran.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks how DVS identifies homeless veterans beyond shelter referrals. Smalls describes coordination with DHS, DSS, street outreach teams, and a veteran coordinator stationed at HRA on Mondays and Tuesdays.
chapters.title: Wilson Q&A: identifying homeless veterans through street outreach

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And outside of veterans in the shelter system or veterans that come to you for help, are there other ways that you are looking to identify homeless veterans that are experiencing homelessness?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Do you coordinate with any of the outreach teams that are out in, that are canvassing the city?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Or how do you identify those folks?

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: Yes, we do work closely with DHS, DSS.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: We do stay in communication with the street outreach teams, but we also do outreach at HRA.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: A lot of times veterans that's coming in to HRA, we have a veteran coordinator that's there Monday and Tuesdays.

utterances.speaker: Donee' Smalls
utterances.text: If a veteran is experiencing housing difficulties outside of being in shelter, we have someone there to assist with that.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks about steps to address mental health impacts for LGBTQ+ veterans amid federal policy changes. Mata describes having an LGBTQ+ liaison, hosting roundtables, and highlighting LGBTQ+ veteran history on social media to counter erasure.
chapters.title: Wilson Q&A: LGBTQ+ veteran mental health support

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And then just switching gears a little bit, you know, in light of a lot of recent federal policy that affects the LGBTQ plus community,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: what steps is the department taking to address mental health impacts and uncertainty, stigma and discrimination for LGBTQ plus veterans?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I'm going to be passing this question to Nicole shortly.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: However, I do want to emphasize that at the agency, we have a LGBTQ plus liaison.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: On top of that as well, we are going to, we have had a round table around mental health and we had LGBTQ plus leaders that indicated

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: certain things that as an agency we can do better to outreach and we are working closely with specific nonprofits and leaders to be able to communicate whether it is through our social media

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: highlight what the LGBTQ community plus veterans have been going through and as a matter of fact we have been putting on our socials

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: the history of LGBTQ plus veterans because oftentimes history is erased and what we want to do is to highlight

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: since the beginning what veterans, LGBTQ plus veterans have been going through and what they're going through now.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So that's one platform and I'll pass over the mic to Nicole.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you for that question and to just summarize also what Commissioner was saying is that we also want to make sure that our bonds with our community-based organizations are strong because we understand that our community is where we are seeing people reach out for services and connection.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So for us if there are issues and there's federal cuts and things of that nature, we want to ensure that our partnerships on the community-based level are strong, including we have a strong partnership with the Pride Center of Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Sage Vets to ensure that we're hitting this community where they are and not making them come to us.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks about barriers stopping LGBTQ+ veterans from accessing care. Mata and Orlando identify lack of self-identification as a major issue, plus federal-level barriers including the trans ban, discharge statuses, and lingering effects of Don't Ask Don't Tell. DVS serves veterans regardless of discharge status or orientation.
chapters.title: Wilson Q&A: barriers for LGBTQ+ veterans and discharge status issues

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: What are some of the barriers that are stopping LGBTQ veterans from accessing care?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And how are you working to eliminate those?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We ended up having, there was a hearing around this LGBTQ plus, and one of the major components is that LGBTQ plus veterans are not self-identifying.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And we, as, and that's why we're working very diligently within our agency to increase that number, because if,

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: LGBTQ plus veterans are not self-identifying, then it also makes it,

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: you know, I don't want to say it's harder to advocate, but it also shows that an agency, we're not doing what we need to do so veterans can also feel comfortable to come to our agency and self-identify.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So within the LGBT, with us having LGBTQ plus liaison and working along with other LGBTQ plus,

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: organizations, we do hope that the number of self-identifications of LGBTQ plus veterans increases over the years and we are going to be monitoring seeing that and I'll pass this over to Nicole.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you for that question and to barriers specifically what we're seeing is what's coming down from the federal level so whether it is the trans ban, whether we're seeing

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: seeing the discharge statuses, still the ramifications of don't ask, don't tell.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: That is something that we are seeing greatly as stigma or as reasons for not reaching out.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: For our agency, we help a veteran no matter what, what their discharge status is, what their orientation is.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: We help any veteran and family member.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So for us, we've been seeing that, and that's what we've been working on, is how do we ensure that we're assisting veterans with their discharge status as well if that is an issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Caban requests a written implementation schedule for each VetConnect Comptroller recommendation, with responsible persons and completion dates. Mata commits to providing it, noting she can speak to actions under her tenure but not pre-existing procurement decisions.
chapters.title: Caban Q&A: VetConnect implementation schedule request

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member Wilson.

utterances.text: Just to close the loop on the VetConnect recommendations from the controller's report that we were alluding to earlier,

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: could you provide the committee with a written implementation schedule identifying each recommendation, the person responsible, and the expected completion date?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: When you can.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: As an agency, again, I cannot speak on what predated me as a commissioner, but I can speak on the recommendations that the comptroller has indicated and what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: To implement those recommendations, but also what we have been doing, the changes within the agency, so we can follow up on that and keep you up to date.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yeah, as somebody that's constantly answering for my predecessor's doings, I totally empathize.
