chapters.summary: Kapner introduces himself as a Legal Aid Society attorney since 1988. He describes Veterans Court as a specialty alternative to incarceration program where participants share military experience, creating camaraderie and mutual support that differs from other ATI programs. Veterans can be rehabilitated because they have previously functioned at high levels.
chapters.title: David Kapner testimony: Legal Aid Society and Veterans Court overview

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: My name is David Kapner, K-A-P-N-E-R.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I'm an attorney with the Legal Aid Society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I've been an attorney at the Legal Aid Society since 1988, and I've been a supervisor since 1996.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I represent, and the people I supervise represent, our clients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: many, many, many of whom suffer from mental health, drug addiction, and that has led directly to their criminality or alleged criminality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And many of our clients are also veterans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And again, there is a lot of overlap amongst those groups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I would like to specific, well, thank you for taking on the issues that you've been taking on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: These are really important issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And unless people such as yourselves take it on and see that the programs are funded and attention is drawn to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: It just won't be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So I represent a lot of people in alternatives to incarceration programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Veterans Court is one of those programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Veterans Court is special, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Everyone's a veteran.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Part of the problem is that getting funded for any of these programs, including veterans programs, is very difficult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: It's a specialty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: The judges undergo specialized training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: The court staff goes under specialized training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I have my...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Counterpart in the DA's offices have also undergone training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: The programs that we utilize through Veterans Court are the same programs, for the most part, that are in drug court or mental health court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Hopefully, but not always, they have a specialized veterans

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: pod or focus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: That's not always the case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: There is advantages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: The Veterans Administration does oversee many of their eligible veterans to sort of coordinate care.

chapters.summary: Kapner describes VA peer mentors who support veterans in court, veteran justice outreach coordinators who help coordinate care for PTSD and traumatic brain injury, and the advantage that veterans' military training prepares them for structured program environments, leading to higher graduation rates.
chapters.title: Kapner testimony: VA peer mentors and veterans' structural advantage

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: There are certain things about Veterans Court that sets it apart from other alternatives to incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: The most important is the commonality of experience from the participants themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: In mental health court or drug court or other ATI programs, people are on their own journey, and it's difficult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: In Veterans Court, you are on your own journey, but you are going down that road with people who have experienced very many things that you have also.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: There's a lot of camaraderie.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: There's a spirit of core.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And in the rough moments when you're trying to, you know, overcome drug addiction or trying to stay on your medication,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: despite side effects and you're dealing with homelessness or other problems, that your fellow veterans are there to help you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And that's not true in a lot of the other ATI programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: The programming that veterans get tends to be a little bit better than other programs that are not veteran-specific.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: If you're eligible for VA benefits, so much the better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Those programs tend to be well-funded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Most of our clients are not in veterans or VA programs per se, but the VA does help fill the gaps and coordinate aftercare and certainly with reporting to the court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Veterans can also be rehabilitated in the classic sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Many of our clients who have mental health issues, have drug addiction issues, come to us later in life, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Like they don't...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Turn 20 or 19 and suddenly become criminal justice involved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Often they're very functional at just the minimal level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They hit their 30s or 40s and something happens and they fall off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And it's harder to rehabilitate folks who have just sort of survived, they've just sort of gone below the radar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But veterans are different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Veterans have accomplished a great deal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: In order to get into veterans court, you do not have to be honorably discharged, but you certainly do have to have been graduated from basic training and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: often been assigned very important jobs, you know, not just combat, but handling jet fuel, handling explosives, even administrative work, dealing with other veterans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: These are very important jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And to the extent that people are coming through a period of mental health crisis or drug addiction, it's just that much easier to bring them back to a place where they've already been, as opposed to try to get them to a spot where they've really never been.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And veterans have a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: A tremendous advantage there, and I think it speaks to the efficiency of veterans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Court that it just really accomplishes really what we'd like to see in all the alternatives to incarceration programs.

chapters.summary: Kapner identifies key limitations: spots are limited by bed availability, only indicted felony cases qualify, there is no misdemeanor veterans court, and crimes with violent components—often tied to PTSD—can exclude veterans who would benefit most. He praises Manhattan Judge Mershon and the DA for considering otherwise-disqualifying cases.
chapters.title: Kapner testimony: Veterans Court limitations and exclusion criteria

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Veterans Court, I think someone else spoke about it before, there are peer mentors that come from the VA that even if you're not eligible for VA services per se, the mentoring program, they're there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They'll call you and they'll check in with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: You can call them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They'll be there in court to greet you, because it can be, as you can imagine, very stressful to be in court and have your life talked about in front of an audience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Not the best parts of your life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So the mentors are there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They're very supportive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: You can reach out to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They will check in with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And it's almost always the same group.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They have, the VA has veteran justice outreach coordinators that can help coordinate care both during the programming and after care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: While they focus on people who are eligible for VA services, they also help coordinate things that are sort of beyond our pay grade, mostly post-traumatic stress disorder and traumatic brain injury, which is something that most legal practitioners

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: don't know that much about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So they can be very informative as that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Also, I'll make this the last point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: As part of their military training, veterans are used to dealing with a highly structured environment, and that gives them

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: a much higher chance of graduating the program because the programs are structured.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And that's something, by benefit of having been a veteran, that they can get the most out of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I really believe in Veterans Court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I think it needs to be funded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: One of my, the complaint I'll leave you with is that the spots are limited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And it's not limited by desire on my part, the DA's part, or the court's part.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: It's the programming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: These programmings have just so many beds, and they're in high demand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: The people who get involved with Veterans Court are people who would otherwise go to jail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So people who are with criminal justice involved but not really facing jail time really don't get the opportunity to participate in veterans court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So there's not a misdemeanor veterans court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I wish there was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Also, as you may be aware, people who suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder, the crimes that they become involved with,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: often have a violent component.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They possess firearms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They are involved in domestic violence, often while drunk or on drugs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They fight with police officers when being arrested on minor things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And many of these things can exclude them from Veterans Court by the nature of the charge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: In Manhattan, Judge Mershon

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And the DA's office understands that to a point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So they will consider people who have committed crimes that might otherwise disqualify them, but it's a heavy lift.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But I compliment them because they will hear me on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So I wish that the program was expanded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Not just in its bandwidth, but the number of spots available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And I'd be happy to answer any questions that you may have.

chapters.summary: Morano and Caban discuss with Kapner the paradox that veterans who would benefit most from Veterans Court are often excluded due to violent charges tied to PTSD. Kapner explains the criteria mirror CPL Section 216 for drug court, requiring indicted felonies, mostly nonviolent. DAs will sometimes consent to violent predicates if behavior is tied to service.
chapters.title: Morano and Caban Q&A with Kapner: exclusion from Veterans Court

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I mean, what I was going to ask you about, you actually started, you addressed at the end of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The exclusion, it seems like the folks who would benefit most from the programming immediately get excluded.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And we see this with mental health court.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It's like if there's a history of an act of violence, even if that act is fundamentally connected to a mental health need,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: directed to prior service and PTSD, whatever it is, you're excluded when probably that's like the most important investment you could make.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Like that is you're making everybody safer by allowing for that participation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I've never made sense of it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It seems more like a policy that's focused on like, will the judge or the DA end up on the front page of the post rather than can we get the person the help that they need to keep them and others safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They are elected officials and I am not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So I don't want to judge too harshly.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'll go ahead and judge.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But, yeah, I think, you know, I hear you on wanting expanded eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And then to your point, you know, it doesn't account for because there's– we're talking about more serious charges.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're talking about– I'm assuming what's the criteria in terms of does it have to be an indicted felony or, like, what's–

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: You have to be an indicted felon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: It has to be an indicted felony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: It mirrors criminal procedure law section 216, which defines drug court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So most often it's nonviolent felonies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They can be...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: You could have a violent felony in your past, and then it's up to the DA to accept you or not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But if you are paper eligible, if you fit within Section 216, which is nonviolent felonies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But, you know, the DA's will have to...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How often does the DA say, yeah, let's do it?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If they're paper eligible but have a violent felony, if they're a predicate.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They can, but how often do they?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Like, is it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Depending on the, I can look at it and say they're going to consent.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I was like, you know, I'm asking to have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: If it's a remote felony or certainly if the behavior is directly tied to your service, they're almost always going to consent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But that's up to us to sort of point that out.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You've got to make the case and sometimes it's hard to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: That can be hard.

chapters.summary: Kapner describes the DD-214 barrier: homeless veterans often lack discharge paperwork needed for Veterans Court admission, and obtaining replacements takes months while clients sit in jail. Morano and Caban discuss CJA interview questions about veteran status, and Kapner notes many veterans don't self-identify due to shame, while some non-veterans falsely claim service.
chapters.title: Morano and Caban Q&A with Kapner: DD-214 barriers and veteran self-identification

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: One of the biggest barriers is many of our clients are homeless, and they don't have access to their own records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So the ticket into Veterans Court is the DD-214, which is your discharge paperwork.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: If you're homeless, if you're living on the street or even in a shelter, that's one of the things you do not have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: In many cases, if your mom or dad are still alive, that's something they do have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They have that with your baptismal certificates in the same folder.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Even if they're not around, if you have an older sister who's the family historian, you can reach out and get it from them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: If you're VA eligible and you have had VA services in the past, they may have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: If none of those things happen, you have to submit a form to the government that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Four or five months later, they will get back to you with that information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But meanwhile, the client will sit in jail, hopefully getting some sort of medication services, but not always.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I know going back to, and this was like a long time ago for me, not as long as...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You know, when we were getting trained on our arraignment interviews, one of the things that we were told to ask is whether somebody is a veteran.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But do you happen to know if that's something that's on the CGA?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: It has recently added to the CGA interview.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Are you a veteran?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I will hasten to add, many veterans do not self-identify.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: There is a lot of shame also of being.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: being arrested as a veteran.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: It's a shameful thing to say, because being a veteran, as you know, is an earned status.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: It's like being a fireman or a teacher or a nurse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: It's something that you've earned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And my impression and what I've been told from my clients is they don't want to drag down other veterans by their association with me because I got in trouble.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So many veterans do not self-identify at that moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And then there's a smaller problem, but significant enough to mention, there are people who will identify as veterans who have not earned that status.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And we have to be very careful as people's advocates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: You know, people are desperate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They want to get out from under and they'll say things that aren't true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And we want to be able to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Aid them by filtering that out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But it's hard to get someone to say I'm a veteran if they're not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Sometimes you could tell from their demeanor.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How they address you, all those different kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is that how they address you in the interview?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Someone looks at you and says, yes, sir, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: That's the next question you ask.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But also...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: There was a time when men of a certain age, you would just naturally ask, or women of a certain age.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: When I first started, I was still seeing Vietnam vets very often, and there were no services in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Once you were involved in the criminal justice system, they just didn't have time or...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Time or energy for you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Post-Gulf War, there was a lot of effort put in, and that's always after military action, there's a spike, and we saw it there.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Right, right.

chapters.summary: Morano and Caban discuss with Kapner the gap for misdemeanor-level veteran cases, where defendants get time-served offers without any conversation about services or housing. Kapner confirms there is no veteran-specific programming for misdemeanor cases and that without significant consequences, attorneys avoid mandating treatment that could lead to failure.
chapters.title: Morano and Caban Q&A with Kapner: misdemeanor veterans falling through cracks

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yeah, the one last thing that I want to ask you about goes, and I asked the administration about it too, is the

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The Veterans Court doesn't account for what we would call just like the frequent flyer, like the person that comes in a lot on low-level misdemeanors, on violations,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: our veterans, and fundamentally the problem is homelessness and access.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're completely failing them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Yeah, we have programming in place recently through cases and other organizations to treat people.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But for cases, you're usually mandating two or three sessions, and it's not like you're getting this person housing or where, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: There is no veteran-specific programming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: They will be more than happy to connect you to the extent they can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: If they become aware that you're a veteran, but it's not like you show up and it's like, oh, you're a veteran.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: We've got something for you over here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And I wish there was.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But on those cases, you saw open arraignments and, you know, you get told, oh, the offer's a violation in time served, misdemeanor in time served.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Ain't nobody having a conversation about anything else.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Oh, I'm getting out right now?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Okay, cool.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: See you later.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I mean.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: With a court mandate comes the possibility of failure, and failure can have consequences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: That is another problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: We seek to protect our clients from those consequences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But that's the thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: If you're facing enough consequences to go down the treatment road, that's what usually happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But if you're not facing those consequences right now, we don't want to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Usher you into a spot you really don't want to be.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But if only folks got the services or the stability they needed before the arrest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: The people who are criminal justice involved because of drugs or mental health, there's lots of setbacks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: It's not just getting them in the door.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: You have to, many, many times you go through treatment and at some point it will stick or something in your life changes and you become much more open to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But it's, we don't want to set up our clients for failure.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Totally.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Totally.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Well done, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Kappner.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I tell you, whatever's in the water at your workplace that produced both you and Councilmember Caban should be replicated across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I do hope many of my constituents will follow your lead in not judging elected officials too harshly.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One point.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Very informative and just such a great perspective on Veterans Court and everything that you spoke about.

chapters.summary: Morano asks what city government could do to expand Veterans Court's influence. Kapner recommends expanding available spots and beds, shortening the screening process to reduce jail time, and expanding the veterans pod within DOC facilities, which currently has a waiting list.
chapters.title: Morano Q&A with Kapner: expanding Veterans Court capacity

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What do you think the city could do, either in terms of the city council passing a law, in terms of funding, in terms of outreach, in terms of agency behavior,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: that would expand the influence and the usefulness of veterans'courts?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You know, one of the tricky things about the criminal justice system is so much of it involves state law, so much of it involves policies of local DA's office.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What could city government do to enhance outreach or the usefulness of these veterans courts?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: I think the standout thing is just the expansion of the spots available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: There's a limitation on spots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: There's just so many beds, and there's sadly a lot of need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So just having those spots available and perhaps...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: The screening process sometimes can take a long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So shortening this, every day behind jail is very stressful and traumatic, and it just makes recovery that much harder.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So to shorten the time between you're being considered for treatment court, veterans court,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: accepted or rejected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Just shortening that time can be very beneficial.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: But I will also say that I know that there's a veterans pod within the Department of Corrections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: And I also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: Last time I checked, there was a waiting list for veterans to get into it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Kapner
utterances.text: So that could be expanded just in DOC treatment for veterans and all mental health, but veterans especially, that would be helpful, that they could concentrate and focus their efforts on veterans.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Kaepernick.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: O'Grady.

chapters.summary: O'Grady introduces Samaritans of New York, a suicide prevention center operating for 40 years with a 24-hour confidential hotline, grief support programs with NAMI, and DOE education. She praises the committee for addressing suicide openly and acknowledges Dr. Nelson and Passaro's testimony.
chapters.title: Fiodhna O'Grady testimony: Samaritans NYC suicide prevention overview

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and it is a pleasure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: My name is Fianna O'Grady, and I'm Director of Government Relations at Samaritans of New York, which is a suicide prevention center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: We have a hotline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: We have a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Program for those who've lost a loved one to suicide together with the National Alliance of Mentally Ill with NAMI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: We do education for the Department of Education for many of the services around the city and we've been around for 40 years and it is a pleasure to have this kind of topic out in the open.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: I think Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Nichols and also Adam's dad and you, I'm in a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: in company of people I rarely am, which is a whole pool of people who are paying attention to suicide and suicide prevention and also for the dignity of those who have left behind with the sorrow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: So it's an amazing...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Accomplishments to be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: today and before the resolution.

chapters.summary: O'Grady presents veteran suicide data showing twice the civilian rate, emphasizes that suicide is preventable and that most attempt survivors go on to live full lives. She frames suicide as a symptom and feeling that can come and go, not an automatic outcome, and calls for nuanced assessment approaches.
chapters.title: O'Grady testimony: veteran suicide statistics and prevention philosophy

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: I would say, listening to the commissioner also, I have the same stat, which is between 2012 and 21,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: veterans in the city died by suicide at approximately twice the rate of the civilians.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: We know that suicide is preventable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: We know that the majority of people who survive a suicide attempt do, in fact, live and who go on to live full lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: So I think also the importance of feeling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: suicidal, having a plan, having the means available, having a time set and actually completing suicide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: I always teach and preach that we have to look at suicide not as an outcome, but as a symptom and as a feeling that is present perhaps at one moment in time, but it is not an automatic outcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: It is not a death sentence, just like if you have a cold, the flu, you have pneumonia, you end up in hospital, you can still come home and live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: If you have emphysema, you might live with it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: You may die, but suicide is a nuanced topic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: It is not a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Black and white issue, it can come and go and so be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: I think empathetic and to have, especially for our veterans who are more at risk, to be able to acknowledge and be proud and to put them in with the Gold Star families is an amazing accomplishment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: It should have been done earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Nichols is fabulous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: You know, to say these things out loud, I think, is tremendous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: When we talk about veterans, we have to talk about families, military service affects spouses, parents, children, caregivers, friends, the people who provide and care for them

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: during and after a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: For families who've lost a service member or veteran to suicide, that impact continues long after the death.

chapters.summary: O'Grady endorses White Star Family Day recognition, citing the Air Force's coordinated community-wide prevention program that achieved significant reductions in suicide, homicide, and family violence. She emphasizes the need for multiple pathways to support, allowing veterans to choose from an array of services.
chapters.title: O'Grady testimony: White Star families and multiple pathways to support

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Recognizing White Star families is one way for the city to see that families should not be overlooked in our city and in our broader suicide prevention efforts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: At Samaritans, our work is grounded in a single principle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: People need multiple pathways to support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Prevention works when it reaches across a whole community instead of resting on one particular service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: The U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Air Force saw a significant reduction in suicide, homicide, and family violence after implementing that kind of coordinated program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: And I've quoted Knox, who after 10 years, they did that study and literally...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: they could see that those who are suicidal, because it was a huge opportunity within the Air Force to study a closed group that you can get back to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: So it's a very significant study, and what it found is that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Helping a person who is suicidal is to allow them to have the autonomy to choose the kinds of support that they believe will support and help them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: So for one person, it could be turning to a religious pastor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Another person won't go there at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: One person will want to go to a psychiatrist and take pills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Another person does not want that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: So it's thinking about it not only as what one thing should we do, it's allowing, it's having

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: options and support and engaging with our veterans to have them choose from an array of services where they will find their maximum support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: And that would be my, you know, big takeaway from the years I have worked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Obviously, we need accessible clinical care, community sport, 988,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady

chapters.summary: O'Grady describes Samaritans' completely confidential and anonymous hotline answering 60,000+ calls annually without call-tracing technology. She raises concerns about 988's involuntary hospitalization practices, noting that those hospitalized against their will are at higher risk for future suicide, and calls for more nuanced harm assessment.
chapters.title: O'Grady testimony: Samaritans hotline and concerns about 988 practices

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: We operate New York City's only completely confidential and anonymous 24-hour suicide prevention hotline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: We answer 60-plus thousand calls a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: And we don't even have the technology to trace a call.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: And, you know, there are 400 Samaritan centers in 40 plus countries worldwide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: And we all believe in that dictum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: And I have seen and we know from the studies, too, to also be careful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: When we absolutely agree that 988 is a brilliant service, but we also know that statistically those who are hospitalized

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: without permission from the person, because they have been...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: they've made the phone call to 988 and the person answering the call, if they determine that that person is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: either at risk for harming themselves or others, then they can decide to trace the call and bring help to that person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Who then goes to the hospital or is in with police, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: And we know that they

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: will be more at risk for suicide and have not learned to turn towards that kind of behavior.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: So I think also having the 988, you know, to continue to have a more nuanced approach to the assessment of harm to others and especially harm to yourself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Is one and that's why I speak about you can have suicidal thoughts, you can have the means available, you know how to do it but you don't have a time set.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: So you reach the edge of the cliff when all of those and so that is like on our suicide

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: prevention hotline, that's our way of teaching and preaching.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: And also, yes, you're calling an anonymous line, but ultimately you're calling a suicide prevention line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: You're not calling, you know, a service that can help you to die.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: You're calling a service to prevent suicide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: And so we need...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: We need a multiplicity of approaches, and I think for our veterans especially, because they're so high risk, it's an extraordinary to know that the White Star family even exists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: I will say that I was ignorant and did not know, and I'm very pleased to learn that, and also from Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Nichols to learn the many.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Nuanced ways of looking at our veterans and being of assistance to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Fiodhna O'Grady
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ryan Graham

utterances.text: And if there's anyone else in the room who's not yet had the opportunity to testify but wishes to do so, let us know.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And as

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Chair Caban noted, I will note that Commissioner Mata has stayed the entire time to listen to what everybody had to say, which speaks volumes about her care for veterans.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Seeing no hands, I would like to note again that members of the public can submit written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So if you're watching this on Channel 79 or whatever the channel is in your local cable provider, and there's something that you'd like to add, you can email us at testimony at council dot nyc dot gov.

utterances.text: And I know she had a family situation.

utterances.text: But I do want to mention Councilmember Palladino, who at a prior Veterans Committee meeting listed all of the potential areas of collaboration that this committee could be doing with other committees.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm grateful to everyone that attended today's hearing, but I do have to say for an issue of this magnitude, particularly when there's over 120,000 veterans in this city,

utterances.text: Had something to contribute.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I mentioned that it could be just as much of a failure of outreach on my part, but I mentioned that because I know the council members that are on not only the Veterans Committee, but the Mental Health and Substance Abuse Committee,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: and these are among the most attentive council members that we have to offer.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And the fact that the commissioner has stayed this entire time to listen to what everyone had to add,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: you know, at a time when I hear the constant refrain that government doesn't listen, I want to tell the public that you have folks that really want to listen.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And if you come to this hearing, and I recognize not everybody can be available to come to lower Manhattan in the middle of the day, but if you come to this hearing

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: and offer solutions and perspective, and we as council members or them as an agency don't act to solve solvable problems, then shame on us, right?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And that's...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I recognize some of this might be cultural, because if there's any group of people that don't like to complain, that don't like to be seen as complaining about anything, it's veterans.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They are, in many instances, the definition of the strong, silent type.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But whether you're a veteran, a family member of a veteran, a health care provider, or anybody that has ideas on how we can

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I really want to encourage folks to please be heard.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I hope that I'm here for 18 hours in that hearing because we hear nothing but problems, perspectives, and solutions that only people that are on the front lines of that issue can deal with.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You know, Chair Lee is a...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I really would urge you, if you're a veteran or know a veteran, encourage them to submit testimony in writing, to come to the next hearing, or to participate via Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And the last point that I'll make, and I'm sorry to go on so long, but...

utterances.text: You know, I'll say this, is, you know, we're considering this resolution on White Star families, and I'm a sponsor of it, and I certainly think we should do it.

summary: Joint oversight hearing of the Committee on Veterans and Committee on Mental Health and Substance Use examining mental health services for veterans and military families, featuring testimony from DVS Commissioner Yesenia Mata and extensive Q&A on VetConnect, Dwyer program funding, Local Law compliance, incarcerated veterans, LGBTQ+ veteran services, and suicide prevention.

Public testimony included Dr. Mecca Nelson advocating for White Star Family Day recognition and military family business certification, Anthony Passaro sharing his son Adam's suicide story, Legal Aid attorney David Kapner on Veterans Court limitations, Samaritans of New York's Fiodhna O'Grady on suicide prevention, and Ryan Graham on system gaps and the Valone Initiative.

The committee considered Resolution 493 declaring April 7 as White Star Family Day, with both the administration and public witnesses expressing support, while Chair Morano emphasized that resolutions must lead to continued action rather than symbolic gestures.
